messages.author: c431c5b9ed1ca911
messages.subject: Configurational analyses using rank data
parts:
Hi all

I was wondering if anyone has any experience, or interest in, the use of rank data for configurational analyses

I am wondering how often are people using fuzzy set descriptions of cases when they could actually be using rank descriptions - with the advantage of ranks being able to be dichotomised at any rank position, not just the mid-point. This enabling more discrimination between competing solutions when the number of cases is limited

regards, rick

messages.author: 53dbab5845ace6b6
messages.subject: Re: Configurational analyses using rank data
parts:
Hi Rick,

I am not sure about the use of ranked data in QCA, but what you describe seems to me a very close description of multi-value QCA (mvQCA).
In crisp sets (csQCA), conditions have only two values: 0 and 1, while multi-value conditions can have more, the simplest being: 0, 1 and 2.
These values can be interpreted as ranks, where 1 is in-between 0 and 2.

So in principle, yes you could insert ranked data into QCA via multi-value conditions.

Hope this helps,
Adrian

Hi Adrian

Thanks for your response below

I have found an example which prompts my continuing interest in this question

It is this table from  Bandaranayake B (2016) Polarisation of high-performing and low-performing secondary schools in Victoria, Australia: an analysis of causal complexities. The Australian Educational Researcher 43(5): 587 Full text available here. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/306330962_Polarisation_of_high-performing_and_low-performing_secondary_schools_in_Victoria_Australia_an_analysis_of_causal_complexities  

Questions: 
1. Are these really fuzzy sets?? 
2. When the minimisation algorithm is applied to this kind of data, does it treat cases with 0 membership value differently from those with 0.33 membership value? Or are they regarded as of equal weight, so to speak. Likewise with cases having values of 1 and 0.67
3. Would it be just as useful, or even better, to convert the above values into crisp set data, using whatever cut off value made sense for each condition - and this may not necessarily be a mid point

regards, rick davies

messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Re: Configurational analyses using rank data
parts:
Hi Rick,

You might want to have a look on chapter 4.1.2 from my book, explaining this type of calibration called "direct assignment".
https://bookdown.org/dusadrian/QCAbook/calibration.html#direct-assignment

While I am not a big fan of this method, and firmly recommend the established "direct method" of calibration using proper numeric raw data, the direct assignment does seem to attract usage, especially because it is so easy to use (perhaps too easy, but that is another story with methodological implications).

As for your second question the answer is yes, the minimization does treat values of 0 as difference from 0.33, in calculating inclusion scores (you might also want to have a look on chapters 7 and 8).

Re. you third question, sometimes it might be useful (and this is very often employed in crisp sets QCA), while some other times it seems like an unnecessary loss of valuable information because all types of sets (crisp and fuzzy alike) are coerced to crisp sets in the truth table procedure, anyways.

Hope this brings some more information,
Adrian
